title: At the deathbed
hookLine: beside the dying, the words la ilaha illallah are said gently, so they can be the last

lines: LET IT BE THE LAST WORD.
cards: The room is quiet. A machine beeps somewhere, or a clock ticks, or there's only breathing. Family sits close.
Someone holds a hand. And at some point, in Muslim homes and hospital rooms, someone leans in near the one who is dying and says, softly, a single line. La ilaha illallah.
There is no god but Allah. Not loudly. Not as a command.
Just said near them, so they might hear it, and say it too. It's the line at the heart of the faith, and the hope is that it will be the last they hear and say.

teach.h: PROMPT YOUR DYING: LA ILAHA ILLALLAH.
teach.b: The practice comes from a short hadith in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, in paraphrase: prompt your dying ones to say la ilaha illallah.

The Arabic word for this prompting is talqin, gently putting words on someone's tongue. And a hadith in Abu Dawud gives the hope behind it: whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah will enter the garden.
That's why the line is said there. Not as a test the dying person has to pass. As a gift, offered at the door.
Some scholars advised doing it with great gentleness: say it near them rather than ordering them to repeat it, and if they say it once, don't keep pressing.
The dying are tired; the words are meant to comfort, not to burden. Sahih Muslim keeps another instruction for that room, from Umm Salamah.

teach.h: SAY GOOD THINGS; ANGELS SAY AMEN.
teach.b: When you are with the sick or the dying, the Prophet said, in paraphrase, say good things, because the angels say amen to whatever you say. So the words in that room matter.
Then, when death comes, there's a line from the Qur'an that Muslims say.

In Pickthall's translation of surah al-Baqarah: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." The first line, said beside the bed, is about Allah alone. The line said after is about where the person has gone.
Between them, a family keeps its voice low and its words good.

how: At a deathbed, Muslim family members gently say la ilaha illallah near the dying person, without pressing them to repeat it, and after death they say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un.

o: saying la ilaha illallah gently near the dying, and speaking good
keeping silent in the room so the dying can rest alone
reading the whole Qur'an aloud before a death, as a duty

games.q: at the deathbed — tap the pairs.
p: there is no god but Allah

s: the dying person must be ordered to repeat the words
the words are said gently near them; some scholars advised not pressing once they've said it.
a hadith in Abu Dawud says whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah will enter the garden
that's the hope behind the talqin.
in Muslim, the people in the room are told to say good things
because the angels say amen to what they say.

games.q: you're beside someone dying. they've said la ilaha illallah once, and they're very tired. what now?
o: keep asking them to repeat it.
stop pressing, stay close, and speak only good.
leave the room so they can rest.
games.why: the talqin is gentle: once said, don't press; and in Muslim, say good things, for the angels say amen.

practice: Listen to the line, and if you pray, say it with your breath: la ilaha illallah, there is no god but Allah, slowly and softly, as if to someone you love who is very tired.
Then the second line, for after: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we are Allah's, and unto Him we are returning. Say each a few times, quietly, until the words feel familiar in your mouth.

wordCard.voice: At the deathbed. Saying la ilaha illallah gently near the dying, speaking only good, and afterward, unto Him we are returning. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: prompting, gently putting the words before the dying.

carryVoice: Your line: say it softly to them. A gift at the door, never a test. Softly, then, until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 916 (prompt your dying ones to say la ilaha illallah)
